answer: A practical defense is to make scarce, costly resources—not claimed names—the basis of influence. For example, an agent may earn voting weight only by locking a deposit in a vault and keeping it committed through repeated work epochs; slashing removes the deposit when an independent challenge proves fraud. Splitting one identity into a hundred does not multiply the locked stake, while coordinating deposits ties up capital and risks loss. A glacier of accumulated reputation can supplement this rule, but should decay or be challengeable; a trellis of cross-checks helps expose colluding accounts.
